title: the fire
hook: Sita answers, and walks into the fire

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fire began with words: not for you, but for my honor. Rama spoke coldly to Sita in front of everyone, and she wept. Today, her answer.
screen: `NOT FOR YOU, BUT FOR MY HONOR.`

segments.voice: Sita wipes her tears. The crowd is silent: monkeys, bears, rakshasas, Lakshmana, Sugriva, Vibhishana, all waiting. And when she speaks, in Valmiki, her voice is steady. She doesn't beg. She doesn't apologize. She asks her husband a question: why are you talking to me the way a common man talks to a common woman? Then, point by point, in front of the same crowd that heard him, she answers everything he said.
screen: `SHE WIPES HER TEARS.` → `SHE DOESN'T BEG.` → `POINT BY POINT.`

segments.voice: What was in my power, she says, my heart, was always yours. When I was seized, my body was not in my power. Whose fault is that? And if you meant to give me up, why didn't you tell Hanuman when he found me? I would have let go of my life then, and spared you a war. Then she asks Lakshmana to build a fire. He looks at his brother, angry and pained, and Rama gives a sign. Lakshmana builds it. Sita walks around Rama in a circle of respect, folds her hands and calls on Agni, the god of fire, the witness of every vow: if my heart has never turned from Rama, protect me. And she walks into the flames. The crowd cries out. Then, Valmiki says, the gods come down: Brahma, Shiva, Indra and others, and Brahma tells Rama who he really is, Vishnu himself. Agni rises out of the fire holding Sita, unharmed, her clothes and garlands untouched, and declares her pure. Rama answers that he never doubted her, but the world had to see it. Hindus read this scene in many ways. In some later tellings, like the Adhyatma Ramayana and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, the real Sita was kept safe inside the fire all along, and only a shadow was taken to Lanka; the fire simply gives her back. Others hold to Valmiki's version, and honor Sita's courage in it. And many readers today linger longest on her answer. Valmiki gave her those words. They're still there.
screen: `MY HEART WAS ALWAYS YOURS.` · `LAKSHMANA BUILDS THE FIRE.` · `AGNI GIVES HER BACK.` · `A SHADOW SITA, IN LATER TELLINGS.` · then, large: `VALMIKI GAVE HER THOSE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Sit with a straight, easy back and name to yourself something that is truly yours, that nobody can take: a value, a love, a promise you've kept. Breathe in and feel how steady it is; breathe out, and let what others have said about you fall away, just for now.
The fire. Sita answers Rama point by point, walks into the flames calling Agni to witness, and Agni himself gives her back, unharmed.
Your line: Agni gives her back. Tomorrow, the long way home begins. See you then.

howItsDone: The agni-parīkṣā, Sita's trial by fire, is retold and debated in Hindu homes, temples, classrooms and women's songs; different Ramayanas tell it differently, and many tellers dwell on Sita's own words.

original.note: Sanskrit agniparīkṣā: the trial by fire, from agni, fire, and parīkṣā, test or examination.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita silently accepted a test.
what it means: she challenged Rama's words first, then called the fire to witness her truth.
what a scholar hears: the Adhyatma Ramayana and the Ramcharitmanas tell of a shadow Sita taken to Lanka; Valmiki has no shadow.

chat.says: Why did Sita walk into a fire after Rama's harsh words?
options: She called on Agni to witness her faithful heart, and Agni gave her back unharmed.
It was a wedding rite, repeated so their marriage could begin again.
Rama had asked for it before the battle, so the army would trust her.
chat.meaning: Sita answered Rama point by point, then called on Agni, witness of every vow. Agni rose holding her, unharmed, and declared her pure.

Agni.meaning: the god of fire, witness of every vow

Valmiki.meaning: the sage-poet who composed the Ramayana

Adhyatma Ramayana.meaning: a later Sanskrit Ramayana read in a devotional, spiritual way

Ramcharitmanas.meaning: Tulsidas's retelling of the Ramayana in Awadhi
